heading: 3 Birth of a Writer
title_zh: 第三章　一個作家的誕生
src: Uchimura’s first task in January 1891 after his apprehensive indecision was to make some sort of accommodation with his school. Those who had noted his hesitation quickly publicized their accusations. Uchimura met with several colleagues during the next week to explain his point of view and managed, he thought, to persuade them individually that the “emperor must have given the precepts ... not to be bowed unto, but to be obeyed in our daily walks in life.” His arguments did not convince his principal, Kinoshita Hiroji. Instead, he counselled Uchimura to comply with a deep bow. The principal felt concern both for himself and for Uchimura. If the latter did not bow, the principal would be held responsible. After Uchimura’s act, some members in the national Diet had urged that, if their teachers could not be controlled, the higher schools should be closed. In his uncertainty, Uchimura sought further counsel from a number of Christians, including Yokoi Tokio (1857-1927), a pastor in the Congregational Church.

Suddenly, pneumonia seized Uchimura, so all consideration of defence or vindication fell on other shoulders. In the ensuing weeks, the newly established news services publicized the event. Uchimura’s action became a matter for comment throughout the country. The advice of friends and colleagues led Uchimura to reconsider his decision, and, finally convinced that the bow was not a religious ceremony, he decided to make a formal deep obeisance for the record. His colleagues published an explanation for his action over his name, and Uemura Masahisa, with whom he had posed along with the visiting Korean in the commemorative photograph of 1883 and by now the editor of an important Christian periodical, came to Uchimura’s defence. Uemura worded his article so strongly that police banned the sale of the issue that contained it. He had written to no avail, for by the time the magazine appeared friends of Uchimura had already dispatched a letter of resignation in his name as he lay unknowing on his sickbed.

But resignation did not end his troubles. The strains that had resulted from care for her sick husband and defence of him against those who wanted to visit him had exhausted his wife Kazuko. She caught the disease as Uchimura recovered and, after an illness of nearly three months, died in April. Her death desolated Uchimura. For the following year and a half, he alternately sought composure in restless trips to the provinces and worked at odd jobs that his Christian friends found for him in Tokyo.

At first, Uchimura journeyed to Sapporo. How he went is not known. One source says that he “walked” (aruita). The same source goes on to say that on the way he assumed a name for fear that he would be refused accommodation at an inn if people knew who he was. His attempt failed because the alias he selected closely resembled the name of a local nefarious criminal.

Uchimura remained in Sapporo less than two months, returned to Tokyo for a short while, and then went into the mountains west of Tokyo, where his brother Tatsusaburô lived. Uchimura stayed there for another two months, writing to Bell, “I feel now just as a man must feel after thunder struck his house. Strangely conscious of myself, weeping over the wreck, and at a loss how to recover it.” He had no great plans, he continues, because “I myself became a burden to my friends and my greatest duty at present is to be able to stand upon my own feet.” The following summer found him on the road again. This time he went to the seashore in Chiba, where he established a church among those he met.

During the intervals in Tokyo, his friends and particularly Yokoi Tokio found occasional employment for Uchimura as a writer and evangelist. In March 1892, he attended the general meeting of the Congregational Church in Osaka. Slowly, hope began to return; he wrote to Miyabe, “here ... with just enough to fill our stomachs with rice and daikon [giant radishes], there burns a flame of soul ... I do believe I have not lived in vain.”

At first, it looked as if Uchimura might once more find a place for himself as a teacher. He accepted a job late in 1892 as principal of a small churchsupported school in Osaka. There he demonstrated great enthusiasm in the service of a cause that could have seemed nothing but lost to others. The few students peddled goods from door to door to pay their expenses. In January, a modest graduation ceremony sent five of them forth into the world. Two months later the school finally went bankrupt. The trustees had apparently given up hope some time earlier. Uchimura later confided in Bell that he always had trouble with trustees and that he had been forced to leave Osaka when he learned that they had invited him “wholly as an experiment!”

Another Japanese whom Uchimura had known as a student in Boston then offered him a temporary teaching position in the western city of Kumamoto. He went there in the spring of 1893, though he had already decided he would return to Kyoto in the fall to begin a career as a writer. Never again was he forced to depend primarily upon teaching for his subsistence.

Nor did Uchimura ever again have to depend entirely on any organized Christian group for his living. During the two years that followed his refusal to bow, his numerous jobs had resulted from the concern of Congregational ministers. He had known them all for a number of years. Many of these pastors belonged to a group called the Kumamoto Band. As students in Kumamoto, they had been converted by L.L. Janes in 1876. Several of their number became leaders in the liberal branch of the Christian church that had affiliated more closely than those of other denominations with the Sapporo church. Their liberal theology pleased Uchimura. It allowed them to ordain the minister of the Sapporo church when no one else would. The same liberality applied to other matters seemed akin to lack of principle. Uchimura could not agree with it, and, when he returned to Kyoto in 1893, he was determined to maintain himself by his own efforts. Even though it seems from this description that Uchimura spent the entire two years after his dismissal from the government school floating from one job to another and full of self-pity, he in fact had discovered a solution that resolved two of his most pressing problems. First was the basic problem of what could be called coexistence: how to get along in a society that did not share his ideals. If he had cherished any illusions that society agreed with him when he hesitated before the rescript, he no longer had such illusions. He needed means of support, of course. Equally important for one so dedicated, he had to work out some system whereby he could live in good conscience among those with whom he disagreed. The results of his decision did not become fully clear until 1903, but he had come to the decision itself more than ten years earlier.

Because he could not work in a complete vacuum, he had to command sufficient respect among his fellows so that he could at least talk with them. Principles alone, he realized, meant little if the person who possessed them could neither earn a living nor effect any change in the attitudes of those he met. He could not become a silent martyr.

Uchimura’s decision arose from his own experience after the refusal to bow. To understand his position, it is necessary to answer two questions: what did that act mean in his society, and how had his personality contributed to the difficulties that his action invited?

From almost the moment of his hesitation, his action became a symbol for something that Uchimura represented only in part: the threat posed to traditional values by the incursion of new values. From a vantage point of more than a century, it is becoming apparent that traditional Japanese ethics were not so much at variance with Christian virtues as some Japanese then believed, but at the time Christianity appeared to be a very dangerous threat to all that conservatives cherished.

Even if the Christian faith itself did not seem a threat, no one could escape the fact of its political consequences. Many of the most articulate among those who desired political change came from its adherents, and a number of Christians had been elected to fill seats in the new legislative assembly, usually called in English the Diet. It had opened just six weeks before Uchimura’s act.

Most Japanese felt great pride in their Constitution and the Diet. Both were seen as visible proof that Japan had achieved equality with other leading countries. Liberals hoped that within this new legal framework Japan could go on to develop a democracy on the Western model. If to the liberal they symbolized advancement and achievement alone, however, to the conservative the same symbols also marked a new stage in the accelerating and fearsome defection from the past. It appears to have been fear engendered by concern over changes that might follow the Constitution that led to the assassination of the young Mori Arinori on the same day as Uchimura’s refusal to bow.

No corresponding violence marred the opening of the Diet, but it occasioned doubts in the minds of many individuals. During the first six weeks, these doubts seemed unfounded, for the members of the bureaucracy who had been appointed by the throne and the elected officials worked together in harmony. This cooperation also ended the very day of Uchimura’s famous act. Within a few hours after Uchimura had hesitated, the finance minister, representing autocratic power, warned that he would not accept legislative revision of the budget.

As Uchimura’s act became better known, therefore, the public became more aware of the potential danger to society that the Diet posed. To the fearful, Uchimura’s act could be taken as the inevitable result of the attitudes expressed by the parliamentary opposition.

If Uchimura had become a symbol of the threat that Christians posed to society, he also possessed a personality that made him a ready scapegoat for conservatives. His act in itself need not have attracted so much attention. Word of it need never have gone beyond the confines of the school. But it appears that he had enemies among his students and colleagues who welcomed this opportunity to embarrass him. His insistence on the attempt to live up to his ideals made him appear prudish and distant. One story, perhaps apocryphal, illustrates how he must have affected many of those with whom he worked. He had accompanied a number of colleagues and students on an overnight outing. As the evening in the inn wore on, the conversation turned to sexual exploits. The teachers talked, and the students provided an attentive audience. Suddenly, someone noted Uchimura’s absence and wondered aloud what Uchimura would think if he could hear the discussion. From a corner of the large room, where he had moved to discuss Japanese poetry with a colleague, Uchimura responded that he had “reverently listened to” all they had said; his icy acidity broke up the party.

Kanzô believed that he had to uphold his ideals to retain his own selfrespect and to provide a good example for the students. Some among them may have been relieved to have him take such a stand for accepted morality, but others must have been embarrassed by his rebuke. They would seek a chance to embarrass him in turn.

To them, Kanzô’s hesitation before the rescript provided this chance. Once word of it spread beyond the walls of the school, others who would have praised his rebuke of the students in the inn condemned Kanzô. By refusing to bow, he seemed to question the only element that gave Japanese society solidarity. He became the scapegoat for his critics’ anxiety and could not easily defend himself because he shared so many of their concerns.

After Uchimura moved to Osaka in 1892, he once more became the object of attack. By this time, he could defend himself. In November, Inoue Tetsujirô wrote a series of articles claiming that Christianity was incompatible with traditional Japanese beliefs. Inoue had the prestige equal to his task. He was himself a new man. After training abroad in German philosophy, he had returned to teach at Tokyo Imperial University. He did not come back to remake Japan on the basis of his new knowledge in the manner of some returned students. Just the opposite; at the university, Inoue used the authority conferred upon him by his training abroad to support traditional ethics or, more accurately, the ethics that the Japanese state sought to make orthodox.

The articles first appeared simultaneously in six Buddhist publications early in 1893. They were later brought together in a book under the title The Conflict between Education and Religion (Kyôiku to shûkyô no shôtotsu). This work set forth the basic conservative case against Christianity. “The disloyalty of Christians results from their attempt to implement their beliefs. Christianity opposes national states. Its advocates consider their ruler like the ruler of any other state. They covertly promote universalism. For this reason they cannot agree with the spirit of the Rescript.”

Inoue’s work brought on a major literary battle. More Buddhist journals reprinted his articles, and the major Christian journals responded. Before it ended, the argument must have consumed tons of paper. A careful count puts the number of books at 21, of articles at 220. On the whole, the excitement mirrored the degree of concern that conservatives felt. It did not die down until hostilities broke out against China the following year.

Uchimura contributed only one article to this total. It came out in the same journal that had first published Inoue under the modest title “An Open Letter to My Colleague Inoue Tetsujirô, PhD” (Bungaku hakushi Inoue Tetsujirô kun ni tei suru kôkaijô). Uchimura first refuted the outrageous charges made against him and then continued with the following argument. You have used poor historical method by presenting only one point of view when you know that good history requires you to judge all points of view impartially. You say we should respect the rescript, but do its consequences warrant respect? Has public morality improved, and do the students apply themselves more diligently? You criticize the Christians, but do you not realize that they act out of the same patriotic motives that animate you? Finally, as a specialist in Western philosophy, you admire the works of Spencer, Mill, and Rousseau. Do they not pose at least as great a threat to political orthodoxy in Japan as Christianity poses?

Uchimura’s argument hit Inoue in a vulnerable spot. Western works of philosophy could not easily be brought to bear against Christianity because they themselves were tainted with its influence. Inoue did not answer, although he must have winced at Uchimura’s pointed suggestion that political pressures – not convictions – had activated his opinions. Uchimura wrote to Bell, “I accepted his challenge, and ventilated myself of all the accumulated feelings of the past three years.”

Perhaps the most interesting aspect of this controversy is that Uchimura did not continue it and did not discuss the main point, which was, after all, the ultimate loyalty of the Christian. He simply asked Inoue to realize that Christians acted in as good conscience as Inoue himself and did not point out that what seemed right to Christians might frequently lead them to conclusions that differed from those of Inoue. That people of goodwill acting in accord with their highest ideals came to differing conclusions vexed Uchimura greatly. In this specific instance, he wanted to lessen the rift between Inoue and himself. One way to do this was to defend his own motivation and to point out that logical use of Inoue’s scholarly apparatus would probably lead Inoue to a conclusion much like Uchimura’s own: that there was an ultimate loyalty beyond the state.

But even to suggest at this time that there might be a loyalty beyond the state invited charges of treason. The state, defensive, demanded complete loyalty, and Christians could not in good conscience give it. All Christians had to solve this problem in their own ways. Almost all the Christian leaders supported Uchimura in 1891 and again in 1893. A glance at their subsequent stands on this issue of state and religion demonstrates the difficulties that it posed for them. Perhaps the most outstanding among them were the members of the Kumamoto Band. They included both Ebina Danjô, at whose church Uchimura had met his first wife, Take, and Yokoi Tokio, one of the first to help Uchimura after his refusal to bow. The American L.L. Janes (1837-1909) had converted Ebina and Yokoi to Christianity while they studied together as adolescents in Kumamoto. Niijima Jô had later inspired them to help him build up the Dôshisha that he founded in Kyoto. When government regulations seemed to threaten the Dôshisha later, Christian leaders such as Ebina and Yokoi gave in. Many subsequently left Christianity to take up positions of responsibility and trust in the secular world. Those who remained pastors addressed flourishing congregations, but they did not probe this question of ultimate loyalty.

The other major group in Japanese Protestantism consisted of those who followed Uemura Masahisa. They did not compromise to the same extent as the members of the Kumamoto Band. At the same time, they did not make a point of their opposition. They maintained their orthodoxy by staying aloof from society. Personal piety and a rigid ecclesiastical organization modelled on that of the Presbyterian Church sustained them.

Neither group therefore kept the problem of ultimate loyalty before the consciences of their fellow Japanese. Uchimura faced the same problems, but he lacked either the support or the encumbrance of institutional affiliation. In the future, he would face the issue clearly when he could. When he could not, he would describe the pain that divided loyalties caused him. At no time did he threaten the deep convictions of other conservative Japanese as he had in 1891. His attitude of cooperation for mutual concern shows up in the last paragraph of his letter to Inoue: “Japan is your country and my country. Wherever we find deceit and cajolery we should cooperate to expel it.”

The rejoinder to Inoue has been introduced to illustrate Uchimura’s basic point of view. Experience had taught Uchimura that head-on opposition to prevailing sentiment merely resulted in the complete breakdown of communication. He always tried to address as large an audience as possible. Once he had decided on this course, he found that he could address with a clear conscience a considerable audience whose members admired him as much for his candour as his ideas. He ceased to write for the general public only when his heightened perception of the immorality of war led him ten years later to retreat from active participation in society. By his emphasis on similarities rather than differences in his defence against Inoue, he set the pattern for his later work, and within this framework he developed relaxed and mature creative powers. Uchimura lived to see Inoue, in his turn, denounced as a traitor by ultra rightists.

During the same two years after his refusal to bow, Uchimura also finally learned how to express affection for a woman and how to show the respect toward a wife that happy life together requires. He had married his second wife, Kazuko, the year after his return from the United States. She was, he told Struthers at the time, a childhood friend, formally untutored but tempered by poverty and by “six successive stepmothers” to “accept all the conditions necessary for a wife of a sincere disciple of Christ, [and she] ... commanded” Uchimura’s “love, honor, and respect.” One practical result of his respect for her was his decision to establish a separate home as soon as possible to prevent friction with her mother-in-law. Unlike Take, Kazuko had not been a Christian when Uchimura married her but became one some five weeks before her death.

Kazuko appears to have been a good wife, but Uchimura does not seem to have appreciated her fully until after her death. In a letter to Struthers that described her passing, he said, a “single woman may not be of much account in the history of the world; but for a man to lose his faithful wife amounts to losing the whole world.” Even when seized by the pangs of bereavement, he thought first in universal terms, almost as if he had not felt her loss sufficient occasion for the pain he felt. He had not even mentioned this marriage or his previous one to his other American correspondent, David Bell. But as Uchimura gathered disciples about him in the succeeding years and began to talk of his past, he told them about Kazuko. He said her grave would become an important historical monument when the educational history of Meiji became correctly understood. He considered her a sacrifice to the ill-conceived policies of the government.

After Uchimura moved to Osaka, he married for a third time. His new wife was the daughter of a famous archer and judge. This man, according to one account, accepted Uchimura as a son-in-law because Uchimura had so many enemies. His daughter, Shizu, was thirteen years Uchimura’s junior. Although Uchimura at first may not have been able to express much affection for Kazuko, from the beginning of his life with Shizu he demonstrated all the warmth consistent with a tradition that restricted display of marital affection to the bedroom. In fact, according to one report, he went beyond such bonds; his landlord in Kumamoto is said to have observed him caressing Shizu in the garden. Uchimura did tell Bell that the garden was “very spacious with all kinds of semitropical plants in it,” and perhaps the plants and the warm breezes of a Kyushu spring had finally loosened the constraints that had so long bound his heart. When Shizu and he returned to Kyoto, they continued to live apart from both sets of parents. The elder Uchimuras did not join them until after the young couple had been married three years and their own daughter had married.

Although readers frequently hear of Kazuko because of her connection with the refusal to bow, Shizu is hardly pictured at all in the historical image of Uchimura. She remained in the background to become what he considered an ideal Japanese Christian wife: one who shared in her husband’s work through her service to members of the family. In old age, he would become pedantic and preachy in public, but in the home and with intimates he had learned both to give and to receive affection with grace. Now with Shizu at his side, he could at last embark upon a productive career. They lived in Kyoto for almost three years. It was a period of great productivity for Uchimura. He published eight books, two of which were in English, and numerous articles, including some that were very long.

Kyoto held many attractions for a writer. Its mountains, rivers, and monuments to past glory provided an atmosphere that encouraged reflective concentration, and its position apart from the main centres of commerce shielded it from the effects of the industrial revolution. Prices rose faster in other cities, and a young author could live cheaply in Kyoto. Hard work, loneliness, and poverty characterized Uchimura’s life there, but the contentment of a happy family and the warmth of new hope made these conditions more bearable than before.

Although Uchimura now enjoyed the delights of a warm home life, he suffered during these years from the particular loneliness of an artist who lacks extensive professional contacts. He did not mix with educators, nor did he teach, except to a few students at the YMCA. He did not attend church regularly and contributed less to denominational magazines than he had in the previous few years. Most of his articles went instead to secular magazines. He also saw little of the members in the large missionary community in Kyoto. Occasionally, Uchimura shared with them a piece of his English-language work, but when he did he frequently returned discouraged over their responses. He remembered these slights until his dying day.

When Uchimura did not make friends among the foreigners in Kyoto, his thoughts turned to the good times that he had enjoyed in the United States. Kerlin and Seelye died, and the news of their deaths must have made him realize all the more that “what I miss here in this land of Far East is that genial open friendship which I enjoyed so much in your land. Here we are on guard against each other.” And there was evidence in the letters from his American friends that he had not been forgotten. In particular, he mentioned the following happy intelligence brought by the postman one day. He had been elected to “Honorary Membership of the Association of Medical Officers of Am. Inst. for Feeble-minded people.” But America and Uchimura’s associates there were far removed. Nothing could alter the fact that during these years Uchimura dwelt alone in Kyoto and communed there, as he later recalled, in solitude with “the waters of the Kamo River.”

Poverty compounded the pangs of loneliness and in part conditioned his every act. Uchimura had no savings. According to one source, shortly after his refusal to bow, the family had to move into a home in Tokyo where a hanging straw mat performed the function of a door. At the time of Uchimura’s third wedding, Shizu was shocked to find that her groom had rented a suit for the ceremony and owned practically nothing but stacks of books and a battered suitcase that he used for a desk. One of the Sapporo chums, Ôshima Masatake (1859-1938), who had moved to Kyoto to teach at Dôshisha, recalls that he invited Uchimura over to his house about once a month during this time. On such occasions, he served sukiyaki; after they had finished, Uchimura would, with suitable apologies, lift to his mouth the iron pan in which it had been cooked and drink the remaining juices. How could any act have better mocked the memory of his brave valedictory in Sapporo? Here, a little over a decade later, he sat almost begging at the table of one of those who had hazed him into his new faith.

Lingering debt made the poverty harder to bear. Uchimura had still not paid all the expenses incurred in connection either with his trip to America or with his illnesses in 1890 and 1891. By 1895, his life in Kyoto had added an extra $400 to that sum. Every day, whether he wrote anything or not, eight stomachs went hungry unless he filled them.

Occasionally, the weight of it made him despair. Once he wrote to Struthers, who had just settled down into a comfortable parish and parsonage, “I wish I could come again to this earth and [be] born again in this country about 300 years afterward. Then they would give me a parsonage or a President’s mansion and a horse and a carriage and a baby too! Oh, Alfred, I am pounding too hard on you, because of my ‘pernicious envy’ (Miltonic expression) for your good luck.”

As his writings began to sell, Uchimura got fifteen cents a page for copy. An approximation of his income for the first two years after he started to support himself by writing, an amount arrived at by multiplying the total number of pages by this figure, averages out to a little over twenty yen per month. This is slightly less than he had received as a student with Ôshima and the others in Sapporo. No wonder that he later recalled dreaming as he wrote How I Became a Christian that he would buy a home by the seashore near Kobe with the royalties that it would provide and retire to write there. Although the poor sales of the first edition of this work provided him with hardly any royalties, his other works began to sell modestly, and in 1895 a Kyoto publisher agreed to loan him twenty-five yen a month against his future prospects. At last he had a guaranteed minimum sufficient to meet his needs and wrote that he was “almost an independent man.” The new ingredient that had come to his life in Kyoto, therefore, was hope. Shizu bore him a daughter whom he named Ruth after the biblical figure he admired as the ideal woman. And he began to have an increased sense of his own worth, even writing to Bell that his publication in the field of Christianity was a “semi-philanthropy ... considering the value of the time of men of my standing (I speak humbly) in this country.” Uchimura seems to have felt a disturbing yet exhilarating sense of imminent change of the sort that often accompanies great creativity. He focused all his energies that it might become a change for the better.

An inner compulsion kept Uchimura at his work. He felt, he wrote to Bell, “driven ... to write about my observations abroad, and convictions I came to in my experiences.” He had staked his all on this venture, and he had to succeed. His struggles to find inner contentment and a wife with whom to share it had given him a special power with words, so that his writings reflected integrity and conviction. In a sense, he had to use his own experience as his chief resource because poverty limited his other resources.

In 1893, Uchimura estimated his library at 100 books; three years later he said he had 150. These few books endured frequent readings and served many purposes. Even newspapers received the same treatment. He had written to Struthers a few years earlier that “I do not merely read ... [but also] study” those received from the United States.

It is difficult to appreciate the degree of intellectual claustrophobia that would close in upon a person like Uchimura who had become accustomed to a foreign literature of a special kind but no longer had access to it. The lack of such sources both increased his sense of isolation and forced him to use his own experience as a major resource. If he was to use himself as a source, he could not do so without imparting a sense of poignancy. It is this poignancy that made the works so attractive. Since Uchimura embodied one of the great dilemmas of his generation, his treatment of that dilemma attracted readers themselves tormented by it. Out of his own painful experience, Uchimura had fashioned the ability to address others in similar pain. Table 1 lists the most important works that Uchimura completed before he left Kyoto. In English translation, they would total about 400,000 words. The date given opposite each item refers to the month in which he finished it; usually, it is taken from his preface. Where possible, the translations for the titles of his Japanese works that he gave to Bell have been listed. The two dates indicated in boldface type refer to secular developments that influenced Uchimura.

These works deal with four themes: lamentation, justification, exhortation, and disillusion. Some lament the pain that Christian conversion brings to the convert. They plead the case of the misunderstood person and sound autobiographical, almost like the first novels of budding authors who can write about nothing except their youthful experiences. They set words to paper in the frantic hope that what so compels them may strike others as worthy of attention. Other works addressed to foreigners and written in English try to justify Uchimura’s background and that of his people in terms that foreigners will understand. Japanese demands implemented in the Treaty of Shimonoseki that concluded the war, he believed, indicated that his people were not prepared to undertake the role that history had assigned them. The Treaty of Shimonoseki disclosed for the first time that Japan wanted large parts of the Chinese empire as reparations to Japan for the cost of the war. The last of these articles of disillusion that dealt with the contents of the Treaty of Shimonoseki gained Uchimura almost overnight recognition as one of Japan’s ablest writers.

The works of lamentation are Consolations of a Christian and Search after Peace. They were finished during the first six months of 1893. This date places them among Uchimura’s earliest writings. Uchimura composed them as works of evangelism to win others to Christianity, but upon first encounter it is their emotional intensity in the description of insoluble dilemmas more than their evangelical appeal that strikes readers. One cannot help but wonder whether the Job-like expressions of despair would attract anyone to Christianity, for they picture not the happy existence that might be presumed to follow conversion but a sense of anomie. In this, they resemble the “I Novels” that began to appear about a decade after Uchimura wrote. Study of some of the I Novels and the men who wrote them suggests that Uchimura’s works may have influenced these writers of what is called the “Naturalist School.” If his works did not inspire them, at least the Naturalist authors responded to the same stimuli that motivated Uchimura. It is best to describe briefly the development of the I Novel and its significance for the new authors before we discuss Uchimura’s work.

Early in the twentieth century a change became apparent in the shôsetsu, the genre of Japanese literature most nearly equivalent to what is known as the novel in English. This change involved, among other things, the nature of the hero. Up to the turn of the century, most heroes could convince their readers as active and effective individuals. They accomplished things in society and thus to an extent moulded it to suit their desires. Although readers might not like Kan’ichi in Ozaki Kôyô’s Konjiki yasha, they would think that, by leaving Miya kicked and weeping on the beach at Atami, Kan’ichi has given vent to an effective and competent ego. To the extent of his ability, he has tried to arrange the world around him in the way that he wants it. As a result, readers could regard him as a personality distinct from themselves.

In the new works that came to be called I Novels (watakushi shôsetsu), the heroes were neither defined clearly nor pictured as effective in society. They preoccupied themselves with the problems of intelligent young men, wandering through a world of bookshops and adolescent affairs, always burdened with self-pity but unable to help themselves. They accomplished little or nothing and shunned society. Their creators did not even give readers their names. This total passivity gave those who read the novels little opportunity other than to identify the hero with his author or to identify the hero’s preoccupations with their own concerns. The hero was not an acquaintance to whose affairs the shôsetsu had introduced the reader. Rather, he was an extension of the author or of the reader.

In a sense, the authors of I Novels reacted against a long-established tradition that classified creative prose writing in terms of an ethical continuum. Elevated prose concerned itself with the promotion of virtue or the chastisement of vice and was the only proper concern of the well-born writer or reader. Other works that did not serve this didactic purpose were considered outside the proper interest of proper people and for the most part attracted their interest only occasionally.

The young authors of the I Novels inhabited the upper-class society that shared the moralistic assumptions of its novels. Through the medium of persistent and dogged translation, the nascent authors had encountered as adolescents European creative writing. It served the interest of art and pleased the reader but did not seem to concern itself with moral issues. At the same time, the whole nineteenth-century Western tradition urged them to stand on their own two feet as individuals but did not tell them how to do it. Most other Japanese could neither supply them with this information nor particularly wanted them to discover it. Readers who hoped to act as individuals found in Uchimura’s early works arguments that both urged independence and pictured the dire consequences of independent action in Japan. Consolations of a Christian describes the solace offered by the Christian faith to one who suffers because he has attempted to live according to its high ideals. At the same time, it defends the author’s integrity. Both his friends and his own lesser self counsel the author to relax and succumb to temptation, but he remains loyal to God at great personal expense. Uchimura’s method of presentation is to catalogue a number of the calamities that can beset human beings. His use of the first person makes his reader feel that Uchimura is reporting his own experience. After a description of the pain that each calamity causes him, he describes the solution that faith offers. One essay is devoted to each of six calamities. They appear to have no relation to each other and to descend unexpectedly upon the author, so that the reader can only judge that fate, or God if he or she accepts God, has ordained them.

The calamities can be divided into two groups of three. The first group deals with the successive separation of the author from those whom he loves. His wife dies, and then both his nation and his church reject him. The second group deals with professional failure. As a result of the failure, the author sinks into poverty and finally falls prey to what seems an incurable disease. Each calamity has its consolation. The loss of his wife leads him to realize that he has strengths within himself and to develop some of her spiritual beauty. Rejection by his fellow citizens drives him to seek solace in world literature. Through this literature, he becomes a Weltmann; even though he enjoys this new breadth, he prays for eventual reunion with the Japanese who have driven him to seek it. Rejection by the church forces him to find his own answers to religious questions and teaches him to tolerate differing views of other persons.

Failure at work makes the author realize both how he could have succeeded had he compromised his principles and how the really great people in history have succeeded precisely because they did not compromise. He determines to act only in good conscience, and as a result he feels himself become a “power for good” who, by his work, will help fashion a better world. Poverty teaches him how relatively blessed he is and how he should not worry for the morrow. Finally, severe illness leads him to realize that God makes those whom he loves most suffer most; it also teaches him that God consoles those who suffer in this way with the promise of future life.

Although this summary discussion of the consolations has required more space than description of the pains that they console, the essays themselves deal almost entirely with the pain and the alternative possibilities of relief that occur to the author. Relatively brief and unconvincing passages present the consolations that faith provides.

Although it is evident that the first and last essays deal with the subject of death, it may not be equally evident that the others take up the question of the individual versus society. How can the good man, they ask, with a vision of a better world, implement his ideals in a nation basically hostile to them? Perhaps he cannot. At the same time that Uchimura urges a transcendental Christian ethic upon his readers, he can be read as despairing that they can find happiness or satisfaction on this Earth if they adopt such an ethic.

Whereas Consolations of a Christian treats an individual’s relations to others, Search after Peace analyzes the individual’s relation to God. In disregard of God’s will, humans sin, and it is the theme of sin that pervades the book. This emphasis begins with its opening lines. “Humans are creatures who should not sin but who do sin; possessed of the duty and the strength to be pure, they are not pure; endowed with the qualifications to make them angels, they frequently sink to the level of beasts.”

The main text is divided into two sections. The first concerns individuals’ unsuccessful attempts to rid themselves of sin. All of these solutions reflect a rational approach and present answers that would occur to a sensitive, intelligent young person. Uchimura begins with a description of attempting to throw off sin either through emotional excess or through neurotic sublimation. As one possibility, he considers the religious revival in which sinners let themselves be caught up in a frenzy and hope as part of the experience to find God and to feel that God has forgiven them. His own experience tells Uchimura that even if an individual gains such a conviction, it does not continue. Only a slow evolutionary development away from the clutches of sin can provide a true solution to the problem that it poses. After this failure to find surcease in revivals, Uchimura turns to social work, where he encounters further disappointment. He learns that to be effective social work must result from strong faith and that in any event it cannot become the means to such faith. One cannot free himself from the toils of his own sin simply by the attempt to help others in need. Study appears as another alternative. The author tries in turn the humanities, science, and theology. None of them provides an answer. The humanities teach much about humans’ happiness but even more about their misery. Science deals only with humans’ source, by which Uchimura refers to the then compelling preoccupation with evolution, but tells nothing of their future. Theology fails because it, like social work, holds promise only for those who come to it with faith. Effective ministers require a very special talent that must be born within them.
No amount of training can make those without that talent save themselves or their fellows.

After his description of these rational, largely academic means to avoid sin, the author decides simply to ignore it. First he seeks peace in the establishment of a “home.” Uchimura uses the Japanese syllabary to express the English word. It is his euphemism for marriage. He finds, however, that a good marriage cannot be had for the asking. It is given rather than attained. Next he decides to adopt hedonism, to relax, and to enjoy sin. He attributes his decision to the influence of the British philosophers Jeremy Bentham and Herbert Spencer. Reading in the biographies of these philosophers who seem to recommend hedonism demonstrates that they, in their own experiences, have not followed this principle. On the contrary, they have led good and sober lives. Uchimura concludes that, even though their arguments convince him rationally, his experience as well as that of the philosophers who have proposed hedonism indicate that it is not the answer. Finally, he determines to try optimism: to refuse to accept the concept of sin itself. Yet he concludes, with a return to a theological position, that such an attempt is foredoomed. Sin does exist; no other conclusion is possible, for it is only because sin exists that humans can understand its opposite: good.

After this long section that pictures experience in each case leading to frustration and disillusion, Uchimura turns to the future. How can one escape from sin? The only way to succeed is to recognize the existence of sin and to desire deliverance from it. To desire such deliverance is to desire to be good. This means to desire to become like God, for God alone is good; our greatest good is dependence on God. The cardinal virtues of Confucian ethics, the basis of Japanese ethics, are filial piety (kô) and charity (jin). Both derive from God’s goodness. People in their original state almost entirely depended on God. Adam and Eve exceeded modern people in this regard until their disobedience introduced them and their descendants to evil and the internal schism of sin. The Bible contains the glad tidings that faith (shinkô) can deliver humans. “Faith is belief in what one should believe without fear or hesitation.” Faith implies absolute trust in the object of that faith. But Uchimura cannot achieve it: “I need proof that God has truly pardoned me,” he says.

Herein lies the irony of humankind’s situation. No matter how much we desire such proof, we cannot through our own efforts attain it. Only through complete dependence on God will we ever achieve the assurance of the pardon that we so desire. Once we have felt pardoned, we can pardon others. Christ’s atonement has already vouchsafed humans the pardon that will enable each individual to pardon others. But we can understand this truth only after we have thrown ourselves on God. Thus, only through faith can we understand the mystery of faith.

Christ atoned for our sins as an extreme example of the partial atonement provided by each individual in compensation for the evil of others. Lincoln’s death by assassination is an example of atonement similar in kind but not in degree to that of Christ. To some extent, each person who pardons another must vicariously atone for the sin of the person pardoned. Such atonement usually takes the form of a good work. Belief in atonement thus becomes the final stage of ethics and the beginning of religion. But in all, Uchimura concludes, we must depend entirely on God. Several features that these works share indicate how they may be considered as precursors of the I Novel. The opening pages of both introduce confusion over the relation of the author to his material that later pages continue. The introduction to Consolations of a Christian states that it is not an autobiography but that Uchimura “represents suffering Christians” and has attempted to console himself with the basic teachings of Christianity. Yet in the body of the work, he uses the first-person pronoun in a way that convinces the reader that it is autobiography. His descriptions seem to lack only specific details. Search after Peace does not use the first person, but its opening lines indicate that the author believed he had written much of himself into it, and its relentless search into the ramifications of sin marks it as the product of personal experience. Readers preoccupied with similar concerns would both feel as if they were talking to Uchimura and see what he said as an expression of their own condition.

Both works also indicate that the reader whom Uchimura addressed was at the same time socially immature and highly educated. The contents assume that readers will see ethical questions only in terms of soaring idealism or dark despair. They will lack any sense of compromise with or accommodation to the realities that experience forces upon even the most dedicated individuals as they mature. It is also assumed that readers will know about sin. They will be concerned about it but will not understand that sin usually results from the attempt to do good or at least to satisfy desires that are not in themselves bad. In fact, the question of how individuals as they develop come to sin is not taken up, and there is no recognition that certain sinful acts might be enjoyable.

If this attitude indicates that readers are expected to have learned but little from living, at the same time they are expected to have learned much from books. Uchimura simplifies his written style for readers by use of a sentence structure that clearly indicates the relationship between its various parts, but the recondite Chinese characters presuppose a considerable degree of literacy. His allusions and quotations also assume acquaintance with Western history, language, and literature. He refers in passing to William Penn, the missionary David Livingston, the nineteenth-century American financier-philanthropist George Peabody, and pioneer social workers John Howard, Elizabeth Fry, and Stephen Girard. He also quotes such Western staples as Milton’s Paradise Lost, Shakespeare’s Hamlet, Goethe’s Faust, Lowell’s The Vision of Sir Launfal, and Carlyle’s Cromwell. They appear along with many other writers who, like the English poets Thomas Hood and John Gay, are now but little remembered in their homelands. Although Uchimura translated most of the quotations from these authors, he did not translate a number of them, and readers must have brought to bear either plodding patience or considerable background to follow his train of thought. In addition, the reader was expected to know the Bible and to accept Christianity and the church as normal parts of life. In these various ways, the works were addressed to members of that group who, like Uchimura, had received an elite training that equipped them to consider themselves both Japanese and Western.

But, as Uchimura’s own biography shows, to feel at peace within oneself in such a state was not easy. One of the most difficult problems was the basis upon which one should make ethical decisions. The official interpretation of Japanese ethics increasingly considered Japanese solutions to ethical problems as simultaneously different from and superior to Western solutions. The Christian norms that Uchimura introduced transcended cultural barriers and required that individuals simply follow the dictates of their consciences. Many other Japanese who adopted Uchimura’s position justified their choice by reference to what seemed the obvious superiority of the West and its people. Uchimura recommended it as the natural fulfillment of the best in the traditional ethic.

One element of his argument was to disown Confucianism and Buddhism as alien. Like most Japanese of his generation, Uchimura said little good about Buddhism, and he considered Confucianism to be the force responsible for China’s inability to cope with the threats that challenged the country. He criticized the “weak ethical principles of China and India” that so imperfectly constrained the animal passions of the Japanese, and he berated Buddhism as an advocate of the status quo when hard work could profitably change it.

Although Uchimura rejected Confucian influence as foreign, he accepted as Japanese much that had in fact come to Japan as part of neo-Confucianism and had been incorporated into the Japanese ethic under Tokugawa influence. Christianity seemed a natural complement to this ethical framework. Japanese who conscientiously followed principles that they had learned as children needed little more to become Christians. Uchimura’s treatment of two concepts illustrates his general apologetic.

As his criticism of Buddhism indicated, Uchimura highly respected hard work and the ability to achieve great ends in the face of overwhelming odds. Another of his early works indicates that the economic leaders in Japan’s past whom he admired most were the daimyo Uesugi Yôzan (17511822) and the peasant philosopher Ninomiya Sontoku (Kanjirô) (1787-1856). Both exemplified what individuals can do when they optimize the skills common to all normal humans. Both had overcome grinding poverty and nursed prosperous productivity from wasteland through their strong personalities, their avoidance of waste, and their application of practical psychology. Perhaps partly because positions of power were so often handed down on the basis of heredity, Japanese society placed particular emphasis on the need for members of each new generation to prove themselves as individuals worthy of their birthrights. Uesugi, who had inherited position, and Ninomiya, who had started from nothing, had each used similar means to outstanding achievement.

The Japanese in Uchimura’s day felt a particular need for the results that would follow unassuming hard work. They saw themselves as poor and devoid of resources, lacking in almost everything except willing hands and hearts. Many thought that Buddhism’s concept that all matter is illusory made individuals less willing to struggle for material achievement that prudence demanded. Christianity as Uchimura interpreted it emphasized maximum utilization of resources just the way that Japanese tradition did. A conscientious attempt to follow the ethics prescribed in either stream of thought made individuals more diligent and capable (majime). Christianity excelled Japanese tradition because it inspired everyone to even greater achievement and made individuals mature quickly so that they could earlier achieve their ideals.

The phrase translated here as “achieve their ideals” is seigi ni tassuru. In the traditional system, seigi or gi represented the unvarying principle upon which all action should be based. Uchimura used it as the English word right is used in “right is right.” Unless one’s efforts eventuate in seigi, he said, they are mistaken and should be abandoned. Since work motivated by Christian principles helped individuals to achieve seigi better than traditional principles did, Christianity made Japanese into better people by both their own standards and its own.

The Christian concept of “faith” was also seen as a more advanced development of a traditional good. It was “belief in what one should believe, without fear or hesitation,” a moral imperative for the individual. To demonstrate the nature of faith, Uchimura analyzed the etymology of its Japanese equivalent, shinkô. The first constituent of shinkô, shin, he found to imply a relationship of truth and trust. Trust depends on truth, and humans must look to God with sincerity (makoto, shinjitsu). Unless each individual possesses purity of heart, he or she can neither trust God nor recognize God’s purity of heart.

Our duty of belief in God and sincerity in our attitude toward God lead us into a relationship that differs from the traditional bond between the retainer and his or her lord. In this feudal tie, mutual responsibilities make the partners interdependent. Christian faith places humans in a different position, like that of an infant with regard to its mother. We must make ourselves able to receive love (ai).

Uchimura, in this analysis of the new Christian concept, relates it to some of the terms most fraught with meaning in traditional ethics. First belief arises from a moral imperative: duty. This concept, with its concomitant of the specific duty for each individual in society, forms a keystone in the familiar ethical framework. Next faith must be based on absolute honesty, with its connotations of purity and lack of pretence. Here again Uchimura invokes traditional ideal norms. Although faith is a duty and requires complete honesty, it can be effective in our lives only when we make ourselves receptive to compassion. The necessity to make oneself receptive to compassion would not appeal to the more self-reliant members of society, but through this interpretation Uchimura reduced the difference between Christianity and native values to a minimum. To accept it still required a leap of faith, but with acceptance the believer merely completed what tradition had prepared for him or her. In a world where change was the order of the day, Uchimura saw Christianity as change for the better in terms of traditional norms. The tone reminds one of Saint Paul. In either case, Christianity is advocated by a convert from the old tradition as a new fulfillment of that tradition’s highest ideals.

Although Consolations of a Christian and Search after Peace illustrate part of the apologetic that Uchimura developed for Christianity in Japan, they illustrate even more the existential problem that confronted Japanese Christians. His experience had taught him that those who took their faith seriously had to learn how to get along in a world hostile, however mistakenly, to Christianity. Uchimura could not take his faith any way but seriously, and as a result it brought him great mental pain. He describes in detail what he did. First he sought authority figures among the Christian pastors, yet he could not completely trust those he found. They did not, he thought, understand his concern and greeted his doubts about their authority with what he calls cries of “Unitarian” or “insane.” In the depths of despair, he then turned to God with the words of the fifteenth-century ecclesiastical writer Thomas à Kempis, “do Thou alone speak to me.” But to request God to decide, he found, meant that the ultimate decision in fact rested with him. Uchimura felt terrifying responsibility and a sense of contingency that might eventuate either in great success or in utter failure. Lapses from his ethical code seemed to endanger the great promise of his faith. He could find safety only in complete reliance on the will of God, and his individual conscience reflected that will.

In the conclusion to each work, Uchimura brings his reader to the same point: the individual must stand alone. In Consolations of a Christian, recovery from each calamity is seen to depend on individual initiative, and in Search after Peace individuals are found to be the only ones who can combat sin. They must resist assistance that others may proffer. Although Uchimura leads his readers to this conclusion, the evidence that he adduces can also lead them to the following very different conclusion. Faced with the social realities of life in Japan, honest individuals cannot hope to succeed. Society at every turn frustrates their attempts to fulfill their ideals. They succeed only as conditions around them change. Fortunately, time works in their favour. In the depths of his despair, Uchimura consoles himself, convinced that “my poverty will not continue forever. I will be freed from hunger when the tides of time change and ‘our period in history’ begins.” The passage from which this quotation is taken sets forth the only answer for individuals who find that society hates them because of their ideals. Alone they can achieve nothing. They believe that they must remain passive, the pawn of outside forces. Such a paraphrase of Uchimura’s words comes close to a definition of alienation, for those alienated see themselves trapped by circumstances over which they have no control and consequently retire into their own little worlds. Although Consolations of a Christian and Search after Peace urge their readers to adopt the new Western way of the individual because it fulfills tradition, by the way in which these works present their author’s own experience they seem to counsel resignation at least as effectively as they encourage individual resolve.

The reader senses that Uchimura felt himself to be in a state of unstable equilibrium that resulted from the very accommodation that he recommended. Although the form that he used reminds one of Saint Augustine’s Confessions, the conclusion showed that Augustine’s eventual calm had eluded Uchimura. His description of insoluble predicament would attract others who felt themselves similarly perplexed.

Selected translations demonstrate the literary nature of Uchimura’s appeal. Consolations of a Christian opens with a passage that portrays the intense pangs of bereavement that assail those who witness death for the first time:

> I had learned about death in physiology; had read of it in the lamentations of poets; had seen it in the annals of biographers; had once actually dissected dead animals in the zoology laboratory; had studied the reasons for life and death; and had at times lectured on death and the afterlife. When I heard of a person’s death, I consoled the mourners either by quoting Holy Scriptures or by describing the deaths of heroes. When the spirits of those whom I had addressed were not revived by my words, in my heart I secretly deplored their shallow faith and blamed them for their lack of understanding. I knew that nothing possessed of life could escape death, that death necessarily followed in a world of living. Further, I realized that heroes in the past had left the world with courage and thanksgiving. I felt confident that I could act in the same way. There was the help of religion, the hope of resurrection. I thought that if some beloved one were dying, I would stand at the bedside singing hymns and reading aloud from the bible. I would bid him farewell with praise and prayers as if he were returning to the country to look after his parents; the separation would be painful, but I would relish the prospect of future reunion, hide my tears, contain my fears and see him off at the front gate with good cheer. Ah! I knew the biology of death and appreciated its spiritual value. But I realized its depth, its pain, its sorrow, its suffering for the first time when its cold hand came to my loved one’s body. In spite of fervent prayers repeated night after night; in spite of my sincere desire to prevent death whether it cost me spirit, strength or life: without warning or pity something that I valued above my life itself was plucked away from my hand.
> Then for the first time I gained an intimation of what death meant.
Later, when Uchimura describes himself as “abandoned” by the church, he starts his chapter with the following passage. It points out the need for people to identify with social groups:

> Man is a gregarious animal; it is not his nature to remain alone. There are creatures like the egrets that fabricate nests on the plains and with plaintive cries strike fear in the hearts of those who hear them; like sunfish who are parasites and live scattered about in the ocean and then occasionally, perhaps for no better reason than to break out of their loneliness, try to fly into the heavens; or like badgers who flee the sunlight and claw out small holes under old trees or between gloomy rocks: here they are born, themselves bear, and die. But man is gregarious like the herring, the cod and the mackerel ... like the seafowl of South America who cover whole islands with their guano; or like the goats who claw their way up over the Rocky Mountains. As the ancients said, an individual man who enjoys solitude is either a god or a beast.
And in Search after Peace, Uchimura pictures the dilemma of those who seek freedom from sin:

> Is there no way in this wide world whereby I, careless of personal gain, unmoved by practical necessity and with the lofty largesse of a prince, may come to forget myself? Not prideful in victory, not despairing in defeat, resting while I work, working while I rest, enjoying the life I dedicate to God and to country? Is there no way to make me into this sort of person whom I idealize? Oh! I live a life of pain. My situation is like that in the Arabian Nights. I cling to one root called life while suspended between the steep walls of this world; below the great snake called death opens his jaws in anticipation of my fall, and a mouse called time gnaws at the base of the slender and dangerous stalk of life. While I am in this plight, my wife and children alone thrive like foliage and sweeten somewhat my fear. Is this the fate for me, I who possess eternal hope?
In the closing lines of Search after Peace, Uchimura borrows from Tennyson’s In Memoriam to describe his ultimate dependence upon God:
> But what am I? An infant crying in the night: An infant crying for the light: And no language but a cry.

In the tradition of Jonathan Edwards that lingered on in men such as Clark, Harris, and Seelye, these words reflected the ultimate optimism. The believer who uttered them was convinced that God heeded cries almost in proportion as they represented sincere dependence. But to those unacquainted with this tradition, the same words could be taken only as an eloquent articulation of the pathos that humans feel when they suspect there is no God to hear their sobs. Depending upon the reader, both Consolations of a Christian and Search after Peace served either Uchimura’s evangelical ends or the contrary ends of ultimate despair. Over the years, many writers who would later produce I Novels read these works and came under the influence of Uchimura. One of them, Masamune Hakuchô, has left a detailed account of the relationship. It indicates that Uchimura’s words continued to stimulate his thinking for more than two-thirds of a century. In reminiscences of his youth, he recalls that there was at the time “almost nothing else like” these two works.Consolations of a Christian was so written that it “hounded the reader” and seemed like a novel (shôsetsu). As Masamune looked back from the vantage point of more than half a century, Search after Peace appeared to be Uchimura’s most important work. There is little doubt that Masamune had found in Uchimura an authority figure. He became baptized, though he stopped attending church before he began to write his I Novels.

When Masamune did begin to write them, his works gave the impression that he had left his Christianity behind in the interest of meaningless individualism. One of his heroes finds that even being loved makes him feel more alone and hopeless than before. In his ennui, he wishes that he might be persecuted, for “isms, books, liquor, women, or even his own ability” do not interest him. Another hero, who has received a bride in an arranged marriage, finds her nothing more than a clay doll. Although Masamune sought individualism as a human ideal, his concern for the human race seemed to have robbed him of charity toward its representatives nearest him. One can only speculate how his own bride, who had come to him a stranger three months earlier, felt as her new husband described the doll in his novel.

Since Masamune had so identified himself with an almost existential humanist position in his works, it was with considerable surprise that his readers learned upon his death in 1962 that he had considered himself a Christian. The perspective of history makes his action seem less surprising. The amorality expressed in his works may have resulted from contact with contemporary European prose that would have appeared to refute the theory that literature should serve didactic ends. Masamune may not have wanted his novels to serve such ends, but he personally sought a firmer basis for ethical decisions. He and the other youths who would write I Novels seem to have found two elements in Uchimura that addressed their needs. The first was literary skill in the description of the pains that society caused men like themselves, and the second was dogged independence in the attempt to lead an upright life in spite of those pains. The young men would never equal Uchimura’s achievement in either regard. The same social pressures that led Uchimura to vigorous faith made those somewhat junior to him and without his faith frequently incapable of anything but inconclusive and ineffective introspection.

To say that these words of Uchimura may have anticipated the I Novel is not to indicate thereby that they failed at the same time as works of evangelism. Many among those who became loyal disciples of Uchimura relate how Consolations of a Christian and Search after Peace helped them to find faith, and Masamune’s recollections show that in them Uchimura could inspire at the same time both a denial of one kind of faith and the affirmation of another, special kind of faith. The Christians suffered under handicaps similar to those of the educated elite, and even the most pious must have thought at times that their faith cost them dearly in terms of relaxed association with other Japanese. Consolations of a Christian in particular said much that they would probably have liked to say.

When these works are viewed as sources of biography, one sees the extent to which despair after the refusal to bow had reduced Uchimura in a sense once more to the position of a dependent infant. In writing out his conclusions, he seems to have freed himself from the constraints that his own despair had occasioned. Now he could turn to address the foreigner who seemed the ultimate source of his troubles.
zh: 一八九一年一月，內村克服了他的忐忑不安之後，首要任務是與學校達成某種和解。那些注意到他猶豫不決的人迅速公開了他們的指控。內村在接下來的一週裡與幾位同事會面，向他們解釋自己的立場，他認為自己設法逐一說服了他們，《教育敕語》「並非要我們向它磕頭，而是要我們在日常生活中遵從」。但他的論證並未說服校長木下弘二。反之，校長勸告內村要深深地鞠躬。校長既為自己感到擔憂，也為內村感到擔憂。如果後者不鞠躬，校長將被追究責任。內村的舉動之後，帝國議會的一些議員曾敦促，如果教師無法得到控制，高等中學校應該關閉。在他的困頓之中，內村向包括橫井時雄（一八五七—一九二七）在內的若干基督徒尋求進一步的勸告，橫井是公理教會的牧師。

內村突然患上肺炎，於是為自己辯護或申明的責任便轉落到他人肩上。在隨後的幾週裡，新建立的新聞服務將這一事件大肆宣傳。內村的舉動成為全國談論的話題。朋友和同事的勸阻使內村重新考慮他的決定，他最終確信那一鞠躬並非宗教儀式，於是決定為了留下記錄而正式深深鞠躬。他的同事以他名義發表了對其行為的說明，而植村正久——他曾在一八八三年的紀念照中與到訪的朝鮮客人和內村並排站立，此時已是重要基督教刊物的編者——挺身為內村辯護。植村措辭之強硬以至於警察禁止了刊登其文章的那期雜誌的銷售。但他的辯護徒勞無功，因為等到雜誌出版時，內村的朋友們已經以他的名義遞交了辭呈，而內村此時仍然臥病在床，對此一無所知。
但辭職並未終止他的困頓。長期照顧患病的丈夫，以及替他辯護、拒絕訪客探望，這些壓力使內村的妻子和子耗盡心力。她在內村開始康復時染上了同樣的疾病，經過近三個月的病痛折磨，於四月去世。妻子的死亡使內村感到極度的悲慟。在之後的一年半時間裡，他時而在往返各地的匆匆奔波中尋求心靈的寧靜，時而在基督教朋友在東京為他找到的零散工作中辛苦謀生。
內村最初前往札幌。他是如何去的並不清楚。一份資料說他是「步行」（徒步）去的。同一資料還說，途中他出於擔心若讓人知道自己的身分就會被旅館拒絕留宿，便假名投宿。然而他的嘗試失敗了，因為他選擇的化名恰好與當地某個臭名昭著的罪犯的名字相近。

內村在札幌停留不到兩個月，隨後短暫回到東京，然後前往東京以西的山區，那裡住著他的哥哥辰三郎。內村又在那裡待了兩個月，寫信給貝爾說：「我現在的感受，就像一個人的房子遭到雷擊後的感受。奇異地意識到自己，為廢墟而哭泣，不知如何恢復。」他繼續說，他沒有宏大的計畫，因為「我自己成了朋友們的負擔，我眼下最大的責任是能夠自立」。隔年夏天，他又踏上了旅途。這一次他來到千葉的海邊，在那裡與所遇見的人們建立了一間教會。
在東京期間的空檔裡，他的朋友們，特別是橫井時雄，偶爾為內村安排寫作和傳教的工作。一八九二年三月，他出席了在大阪舉行的公理教會全體大會。希望慢慢地開始回歸；他寫信給宮部金吾說：「這裡……僅僅有足夠的白飯和蘿蔔充飢，但靈魂的火焰在熊熊燃燒……我確實相信我沒有白活。」

起初，內村似乎有望再次以教師身分找到自己的立足點。一八九二年末，他接受了一份工作，擔任大阪一所教會支持的小學校的校長。在那裡，他為一項對他人來說似乎已經完全絕望的事業表現出巨大的熱情。為數不多的學生挨戶販賣商品來支付他們的開銷。一月時，一場簡樸的畢業典禮送出了其中五名學生進入社會。兩個月後，學校終於破產了。董事會顯然早就放棄了希望。內村後來向貝爾坦白，他向來與董事會相處困難，當他得知他們邀請他來「完全只是作為實驗」時，被迫離開了大阪。
另有一位曾在波士頓與內村同為學生的日本人，此時向他提供了熊本西部城市的臨時教職。一八九三年春，內村前往就任，雖然他早已決定將在秋季返回京都，開始以寫作為生。自此以後，他再也不必依靠教職作為主要生計了。

內村鑑三從此也不必再完全依賴任何有組織的基督教團體來維持生計。在他拒絕鞠躬後的兩年間，他眾多的工作機會都來自公理會牧師們的關心。他與這些牧師已相識多年。其中許多牧師屬於一個名叫熊本帶的團體。他們在熊本求學時，曾於一八七六年被L‧L‧詹姆士所歸正。其中數人成為基督教自由派分支的領導人物，而該派與札幌教會的聯繫比其他教派更密切。他們的自由派神學令內村鑑三心悅誠服。正是這種自由主義精神使他們願意按立札幌教會的牧師，當其他人都不願意的時候。但這種自由主義應用於其他事務上時，似乎與缺乏原則相近。內村鑑三不能同意這一點。一八九三年當他返回京都時，他已下定決心要靠自己的力量維持生活。 雖然從以上的敘述看來，內村鑑三在被政府學校開除後的整個兩年裡似乎在四處奔波找工作，滿懷自憐，但事實上他已經發現了一個解決方案，它解決了他最迫切的兩個問題。首先是一個可稱之為「共存」的根本問題：如何在一個不認同自己理想的社會中生活。如果他在猶豫是否要對敕語鞠躬時還懷抱著社會贊同他的任何幻想，現在他已經不再有這樣的幻想。當然，他需要經濟來源。但對於一個如此獻身的人來說，同樣重要的是，他必須想出某個制度，使自己能夠坦然地生活在與他意見相左的人們之間。他這個決定的結果直到一九〇三年才完全顯現，但他本人在十多年前就已經做出了這個決定。
因為他不可能在完全的真空中工作，所以必須贏得同儕之間足夠的尊重，至少能夠與他們對話。他意識到，單純的原則意義不大，如果擁有這些原則的人既無法謀生，也無法改變他所接觸的人的態度。他不能成為無聲的殉難者。
內村的決定源自他拒絕鞠躬後的親身經歷。要理解他的立場，必須回答兩個問題：在他所處的社會中，那個舉動意味著什麼？以及他的性格如何促成了他的行為所招致的困難？
從他那片刻的遲疑開始，他的行動便成為了一個象徵——象徵內村只在一定程度上所代表的東西：新價值觀的入侵對傳統價值觀所構成的威脅。站在超過一個世紀的距離看待這段歷史，人們逐漸發現傳統日本倫理與基督教美德的差異並不如當時某些日本人所相信的那麼大，但在那個時代，基督教對於保守派珍視的一切看起來都是一個極其危險的威脅。
即便基督教信仰本身似乎不構成威脅，但沒有人能逃避其政治後果這一事實。在那些渴望政治變革、最善於言辭的人物中，許多出自基督教信徒之列；而且有若干基督徒當選進入新成立的立法議會——英文通常稱之為帝國議會。該議會開幕於內村事件發生前的短短六週。

大多數日本人對自己的憲法和帝國議會感到極大的自豪。兩者都被視為日本已達成與其他先進國家平等地位的有形證明。自由主義者希望在這個新的法律框架內，日本能繼續發展西方式的民主制度。然而，如果對自由主義者而言，這些象徵僅代表進步與成就，對保守派而言，同樣的象徵也標誌著一個新的階段——過去正在加速且令人恐懼地被背棄。看起來，正是對憲法實施可能引發之變化的關切所激起的恐懼，導致了年輕的森有禮在與內村拒絕敬禮同一天遭到暗殺的事件。
帝國議會的開幕雖未發生相應的暴力事件，但卻引起許多人心中的疑慮。在最初六週內，這些疑慮似乎毫無根據，因為由天皇任命的官僚及民選議員之間合作無間。這種合作也正好在內村製造聞名事件的當日告終。內村猶豫之後不過數小時，代表專制權力的財務大臣就警告說，他將不接受立法機構對預算的修改。
隨著內村的舉動廣為人知，社會大眾因而愈加意識到帝國議會對社會構成的潛在危險。對於那些心懷恐懼的人來說，內村的舉動可被視為國會反對派所表達之態度的必然結果。

如果內村已經成為基督徒對社會構成威脅的象徵，他的個性也使他成為保守派容易發洩的替罪羊。他的行為本身未必會引起那麼多關注。風聲本來根本不必傳出學校以外。但似乎他在學生和同事中有敵人，他們歡迎這個機會來為難他。他堅持要實踐自己的理想，這使他看起來既端莊保守又疏遠冷漠。有一個故事或許不足為信，卻說明了他必定對許多與他共事的人造成的影響。他曾與一些同事和學生一起參加過夜的郊遊。當晚間在旅館裡的時光逐漸深入，談話轉向了性的冒險經歷。教師們高談闊論，學生們則做著專注的聽眾。突然，有人注意到內村不在，大聲想知道內村聽到這番談話會作何感想。內村從房間的一角——他曾在那裡和一位同事討論日本詩歌——回應說，他已經「恭敬地傾聽」了他們所說的一切；他那刀子般冷酷的諷刺評論頓時掃興了整場聚會。
鑑三相信，為了維護自身的尊嚴，也為了給學生樹立良好榜樣，他必須堅守自己的理想。學生中有些人可能因為他為公認的道德倫理挺身而出而感到寬慰，但也有些人勢必對他的訓斥感到尷尬。他們會伺機反過來讓他難堪。
對他們而言，鑑三在敕語前的遲疑提供了這個機會。一旦消息傳出校園外牆，那些本會讚揚他斥責旅舍學生的人紛紛譴責鑑三。他拒絕鞠躬，彷彿質疑了唯一給予日本社會團結的要素。他成了評論者焦慮的代罪羔羊，而且難以自衛，因為他本身對許多問題抱持著與批評者相同的關懷。

內村於一八九二年遷居大阪後，再度成為攻擊的對象。此時他已能自我防衛。十一月，井上哲次郎撰文一系列論文，聲稱基督教與日本傳統信仰不相容。井上哲次郎具備勝任此任的聲望。他本身也是新人物。在國外接受過德國哲學訓練後，他回國在東京帝國大學教學。他並未如某些留學歸來的學生那樣，企圖以新知識為基礎改造日本。恰恰相反；在大學裡，井上哲次郎利用其海外訓練所賦予他的權威，來維護傳統倫理，或更準確地說，維護日本國家所設法建立的正統倫理。
這些文章最初於一八九三年初同時刊登在六份佛教刊物上。隨後被匯集成一部著作，書名為《教育與宗教的衝突》（教育と宗教の衝突）。這部著作闡述了反對基督教的基本保守立場。「基督徒的不忠誠源於他們試圖踐行自己的信仰。基督教反對民族國家。其倡導者視自己的統治者如同任何其他國家的統治者。他們暗中推行普遍主義。因此他們無法認同教育敕語的精神。」
井上哲次郎的著作引發了一場重大的文字論戰。許多佛教刊物轉載他的文章，主要的基督教刊物也隨之應戰。這場爭論到了尾聲時，必然耗費了大量的紙張。仔細計算下來，著作達二十一部，文章達二百二十篇。總的來說，這場論戰的熱烈程度反映了保守派所感受到的深切憂慮。直到隔年對華動武爆發，這場爭論才告平息。

內村只為此總集貢獻了一篇文章。該文發表在最初刊登井上文章的同一家刊物上，題目謙遜地定為〈致吾友井上哲次郎博士公開信〉（《文學博士井上哲次郎君に呈する公開狀》）。內村先是駁斥了針對自己的荒謬指控，隨後繼續論述如下：你採用了拙劣的歷史方法，明知良好的歷史著述要求人們公正無偏地評判所有觀點，卻只呈現了一家之言。你說我們應當尊重敕語，但敕語的後果是否值得尊重？民間道德是否改善了，學生是否更勤奮地自我砥礪？你批評基督徒，但你是否沒有意識到他們的愛國動機與你自己的動機完全相同？最後，作為西方哲學的專家，你敬慕斯賓塞、穆勒和盧梭的著作。這些人的思想難道不至少與基督教一樣對日本的政治正統性構成威脅？
內村的論證擊中了井上哲次郎的痛點。西方哲學著作無法輕易用來反對基督教，因為它們本身就已經被基督教的影響所玷污。井上沒有回應，但他必定對內村那尖銳的暗示感到難受——即政治壓力而非信念才驅動了他的言論。內村寫信給貝爾說：「我接受了他的挑戰，傾瀉了過去三年積累的全部感受。」

這場爭論中最值得關注的或許是，內村並未繼續這場論戰，也未深入探討其核心問題——畢竟那涉及基督徒最終的忠誠歸屬。他只是要求井上哲次郎認識到，基督徒的行動出於與井上本人同樣清淨的良心，卻未指出：對基督徒而言似乎正確的立場，往往會引他們走向不同於井上的結論。志同道合的人們按照各自最高的理想行動，卻得出相異的結論，這令內村極感困擾。在這一具體事例中，他希望彌合井上與自己之間的分歧。為此，他採取的一個方式是為自己的動機辯護，並指出：若邏輯地運用井上本人的學術方法，井上多半會得出與內村相近的結論——即存在著超越國家之外的最終忠誠。

但即使在這個時刻只是暗示國家之外可能存在某種忠誠，都會招致背叛的指控。國家處於防守狀態，要求絕對忠誠，而基督徒無法憑著良心給予這樣的忠誠。所有基督徒都必須以各自的方式解決這個問題。幾乎所有基督教領袖都在一八九一年和一八九三年支持內村。審視他們在這個國家與宗教問題上的後續立場，便可看出它對他們造成的困境。其中最傑出的人物或許是熊本帶的成員。他們包括海老名彈正——內村在其教會裡認識了他的第一任妻子竹子——和橫井時雄，後者是最早在內村拒絕鞠躬後幫助他的人之一。美國人L.L.詹姆斯（一八三七─一九〇九）曾在熊本時與他們一起研習時將海老名和橫井歸信基督教。新島襄後來激勵他們幫助他在京都建立所創辦的同志社。當政府法令日後似乎威脅到同志社時，海老名和橫井等基督教領袖屈服了。許多人隨後離開基督教，轉而在世俗世界裡擔任責任重大、受信任的職位。那些仍為牧師的人牧養著興旺的教會，但他們並未深入探討這個最終忠誠的問題。
日本新教中的另一大派系是追隨植村正久的人士。他們不像熊本洋學校出身者那樣做出讓步。但同時，他們也不刻意標榜反對立場。他們透過與社會保持距離來維持正統信仰。個人虔誠與仿照長老教會組織形式建立的嚴格教會體制支撐了他們。

因此，兩派都沒有把終極忠誠的問題放在同胞的良心面前。內村鑑三面臨著同樣的問題，但他既缺乏制度隸屬所帶來的支持，也不受其牽累。將來，他在有機會時會直率地面對這個問題。在沒有機會時，他會描述分裂的忠誠給他帶來的痛苦。他再也沒有像一八九一年那樣威脅其他保守派日本人根深蒂固的信念。他為了相互關切而合作的態度體現在他寫給井上的信的最後一段：「日本是你的國家，也是我的國家。無論我們在何處發現欺瞞和哄騙，都應當合作將其驅逐出去。」

對井上的駁論已在前面引用，用以說明內村的基本觀點。經驗教會了內村，與流行的輿論正面對立，其結果只能是溝通的完全破裂。他總是力圖面對盡可能廣大的聽眾。一旦採取了這個方針，他發現自己可以無愧地面對一個相當龐大的聽眾，這些人欽佩他既是為了他的坦率，也是為了他的思想。十年後，當他對戰爭的不道德性的認識加深，促使他從社會的積極活動中退隱時，他才停止為一般大眾寫作。在對井上的辯護中，他強調相似之處而非差異，這為他後來的工作奠定了基調，在這個框架內，他發展了放鬆而成熟的創造力。內村活著看到了井上本人也被極端右翼分子斥為叛徒的一幕。

在拒絕行禮後的同樣兩年間，內村也終於學會了如何對女性表示感情，以及如何對妻子表現出幸福生活所需的尊重。他在從美國回國後的第二年娶了第二任妻子和子。他曾向施魯瑟斯說，她是童年時期的朋友，雖然沒有受過正規教育，但貧困和「六個繼母」相繼的經歷使她能夠「接受基督忠實門徒之妻所必需的一切條件，[她]……贏得了」內村的「愛、尊敬與敬重」。他對她的尊重所產生的一個實際結果是他決定盡早建立獨立的家庭，以防止與婆婆之間發生摩擦。不同於武，和子在內村娶她時還不是基督徒，但在去世前約五週時才成為了基督徒。

和子看來是個賢慧的妻子，但內村似乎直到她去世後才充分欣賞她。在一封給斯特拉瑟斯描述她去世的信中，他說：「一個女人在世界歷史上或許無足輕重；但男子失去忠貞的妻子，無異於失去整個世界。」即使在喪慟的劇痛中，他也首先用普遍的眼光思考，彷彿他所感受到的痛楚並非源於失去她本身。他甚至沒有向另一位美國通信者大衛‧貝爾提及過他的這段婚姻或之前的那段婚姻。但隨著內村在其後歲月裡聚集了弟子，開始談論他的過去，他就向他們講述了和子的故事。他說，當人們正確認識了明治教育史時，她的墓將成為一個重要的歷史紀念碑。他認為她是政府錯誤政策的犧牲者。

內村遷居大阪後，第三次結婚。新妻是一位著名箭手兼法官的女兒。根據一個說法，這位岳父之所以接納內村為女婿，是因為內村敵人眾多。他的女兒志津比內村年輕十三歲。儘管內村起初可能無法對和子表達太多的感情，但從與志津生活的開始，他就表現出與傳統相符的溫情——傳統將夫妻間的親密限制在臥房之內。事實上，根據一份記載，他超越了這樣的界限；據說他在熊本的房東曾看到他在花園裡撫摸志津。內村確實對貝爾說過那花園「非常寬敞，種著各種亞熱帶植物」，或許是那些植物和九州春天溫暖的微風，終於鬆開了長久以來束縛著他心靈的枷鎖。當志津與他回到京都時，他們繼續與雙方父母分開居住。直到年輕夫婦結婚三年之後，他們自己的女兒也已婚配，內村的父母才搬來與他們同住。

雖然讀者常因和子與不敬事件的關連而聽聞其名，但志津在內村的歷史形象中幾乎完全隱沒。她甘居幕後，成為內村心目中理想的日本基督教妻子：通過對家庭成員的服侍，在丈夫的事業中有所參與。年長之後，他在公開場合變得迂腐而說教，但在家庭裡和親近的人相處時，他已學會優雅地既給予又接納感情。如今有志津在側，他終於能夠開始一段富有成果的事業生涯。他們在京都住了將近三年。這是內村極具生產力的時期。他出版了八部著作，其中兩部以英文寫就，並發表了許多文章，其中一些篇幅很長。
京都對於一位作家有很多吸引力。它的山川和過往榮光的紀念碑提供了鼓勵沉思專注的氛圍，而它遠離主要商業中心的位置使它免受工業革命的影響。其他城市的物價上升更快，年輕的作家可以在京都低廉地生活。艱苦的工作、孤獨和貧困這些條件曾經主宰了內村在京都的生活，但家庭幸福帶來的滿足感和新希望的溫暖使得這些境遇比以前更加可以忍受。

雖然內村如今享受著溫暖家庭生活的喜悅，但在這些年間，他卻飽受一位缺乏廣泛專業人脈的藝術家所特有的孤獨。他不與教育工作者交往，也不從事教學，除了在基督教青年會教幾名學生外。他不經常參加教會禮拜，投稿教派雜誌的頻率也遠不如前幾年。他的大部分文章改投世俗雜誌。他也很少與京都龐大的宣教士群體中的成員往來。內村偶爾會與他們分享自己的英文著作，但每次這樣做時，他往往因為他們的反應而沮喪地離開。這些冷遇在他的記憶中一直留到生命的最後一刻。

內村在京都未能與外國人建立友誼，思想便轉向在美國享受過的美好時光。克拉克與席利相繼去世，這些訃聞必然令他更加體悟到「我在這遠東之地所懷念的，就是我在你們國土上所享受的那種親切開放的友誼。這裡我們互相戒備。」而他美國友人的來信證明他並未被遺忘。他尤其提及郵差某日帶來的這樁令人欣喜的消息：他被選為「美國智能遲緩者研究所醫療人員協會榮譽會員」。然而美國和內村在那裡的友人相距遙遠。沒有什麼能改變這樣的事實：在這些年月中，內村獨自棲居於京都，並如他後來所回憶的，在那裡獨處而與「鴨川的水流」相伴。

貧窮加重了孤獨的痛楚，並在某種程度上制約著他的每一個舉動。內村沒有積蓄。據某個史料記載，在他拒絕鞠躬後不久，全家不得不搬進東京的一間房子，那裡只用一條懸掛的草蓆充當門。到了內村第三次結婚時，志津驚訝地發現新郎租用了一套禮服參加典禮，實際上除了成堆的書籍和一只破舊的旅行箱（他用來當書桌）外，一無所有。札幌農學校時期的同窗大島正武（1859-1938）後來移居京都在同志社教書，他回憶說在那段時期大約每月邀請內村去家裡一次。在這樣的場合裡，他會招待壽喜燒；用完餐後，內村會帶著適當的道歉，把煮菜用的鐵鍋舉到嘴邊，喝盡裡面剩下的湯汁。還有什麼舉動能比這更嘲諷他在札幌時那勇敢的離別辭呢？十多年後的此刻，他幾乎是在向那些當年把他推向新信仰的人之一的餐桌前乞求。
揮之不去的債務使貧困更難以忍受。內村至今尚未償清與赴美之行以及一八九○至一八九一年間患病相關的所有開支。到一八九五年，他在京都的生活又增加了四百美元的債務。每天，無論他是否寫作，如果他不填飽肚子，八張嘴就會挨餓。
有時候，這種重擔使他感到絕望。他曾寫信給已經安頓在舒適牧師館和教區中的史特拉瑟斯，說：「我但願能再次降生於人世，在這個國家三百年後重新誕生。那時他們會給我一個牧師館或總統公館，還有馬匹、馬車和孩子！哦，艾爾弗雷德，我對你發洩太多怨氣了，因為對你的好運有著『惡毒的嫉妒心』（米爾頓式的表達）。」

隨著著作開始銷售，內村每頁稿費得到十五美分。根據他開始以寫作自給自足後頭兩年的收入估計——以總頁數乘以這個數字算出——平均每月略超過二十圓。這略少於他在札幌跟大島等人讀書時所獲得的。難怪他後來回憶起在寫作《我如何成為基督徒》時夢想著，能用該書的版稅在神戶附近海濱買一棟房子，然後隱居在那裡寫作。儘管該作第一版銷售不佳，給他帶來的版稅寥寥無幾，但他的其他著作開始有了適度的銷售，到了一八九五年，京都的一家出版商同意每月預支他二十五圓，以他未來的發展前景作為擔保。終於，他有了足夠應付需要的保證最低生活費，並寫下自己是「幾乎是個獨立的人」。因此，來到京都生活中的新元素是希望。靜子為他生了一個女兒，他取名為路得，以這位他敬佩為理想女性的聖經人物命名。他也開始對自己的價值有了增強的認識，甚至寫信給貝爾說，他在基督教領域的出版是「半慈善事業……考慮到本國像我這樣身分的人的時間價值（我言之謙卑）」。內村似乎感受到了一種既令人不安又令人興奮的迫在眉睫變化的感覺，這種感覺往往伴隨著偉大的創意而來。他集中所有精力，使其成為更好的改變。
內村被一股內在的衝動驅使著繼續工作。他在給貝爾的信中寫道，他感到「被驅使著去寫下我在國外的觀察，以及我在經歷中所得到的信念」。他把一切都賭在了這個事業上，他必須成功。他為尋求內心的平靜和一位與之分享生命的妻子所經歷的掙扎，賦予了他特殊的文字力量，因此他的著作反映出真摯與信念。從某種意義上說，他必須把自己的經驗作為主要資源，因為貧困限制了他其他的資源。
一八九三年，內村估計他的藏書約有一百冊；三年後他說已有一百五十冊。這些為數不多的書籍經常被反覆翻閱，用途頗多。即便報紙也得到同樣的對待。他曾在數年前寫信給施魯瑟斯說，他不僅是「閱讀」從美國寄來的報刊，「而是深入研究」。

對於像內村這樣已經習慣於接觸某類外國文獻、卻突然失去這種途徑的人來說，很難體會那種知識上的幽閉恐怖。這類資源的缺乏既加深了他的孤立感，又迫使他將自身經歷作為主要的思想資源。如果他要以自己為源泉，就無法避免帶上一種蒼涼的意味。正是這種蒼涼，使他的著作具有吸引力。由於內村本身體現了他那一代人的重大困境，他對這一困境的處理方式吸引了同樣為之所困的讀者。內村以自己的痛苦經歷，磨練出向同樣苦難中的人們傾訴的能力。表1列舉了內村離開京都前完成的最重要著作。這些著作用英文翻譯的話，合計約四十萬詞。各項條目旁標注的日期指他完成該著作的月份；通常取自他的序文。凡有可能，都採用了他向貝爾提供的日文著作標題的英譯版本。以粗體標注的兩個日期指影響了內村的世俗事件。

這些著作涉及四個主題：哀歎、申辯、勸勉和幻滅。有些作品哀歎基督教歸信給歸信者所帶來的痛苦。它們為被人誤解的個人辯護，帶有自傳色彩，幾乎像初出茅廬的作家所寫的第一部小說，除了青年時代的經歷外無他所寫。作者匆匆將言語訴諸筆端，希望自己深感所迫的事物也能令他人覺得值得關注。另有一些作品是為外國人而作，用英文寫成，試圖用外國人能理解的語言為內村的背景和他民族的特性進行申辯。當人們得知其中一部著作也成為日文譯本的經典之作時，這些著作的重要性便更加凸顯。第三類作品涉及世界歷史，並勸勉
